title: Senior's toolkit: writing and tracing queries
summary: Projections, no-tracking reads, safe raw SQL, LIKE, compiled queries and tags that let you find a query in a database trace.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: writing and tracing queries
steps.body: Most EF Core performance and security problems are in how queries are written. These are the APIs experienced developers use to read only what they need, keep raw SQL safe, and find their query in a busy database.

toolkit.what: Project straight into the shape the caller needs. Only those columns are read, and nothing is tracked.
flags: Select into a record or DTO
EF Core writes the JOIN for you, no Include needed
toolkit.example: await db.Books.Select(b => new BookRow(b.Id, b.Title, b.Author.Name)).ToListAsync(ct);

toolkit.what: Read entities without tracking them. Faster and uses less memory for read-only work such as API GETs and reports.
flags: no tracking; the same row twice gives two objects
no tracking, but one object per row
make it the default for the context

toolkit.what: Run your own SQL safely. Interpolated values become parameters, never pasted text, so they cannot inject SQL.
flags: plain string; only with constant SQL and explicit parameters
map raw SQL to a type that is not an entity
toolkit.example: db.Books.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Books WHERE Author = {author}").Where(b => b.Year > 2000)

toolkit.what: SQL LIKE inside LINQ, with `%` and `_` wildcards. `EF.Functions` holds other database functions too.
Put a comment at the top of the generated SQL. A DBA looking at a slow-query report can then see which code sent it.
flags: adds the file and line that built the query
toolkit.example: db.Orders.TagWith("Orders page: open orders").Where(o => o.Status == Status.Open)
toolkit.when: any query that might show up in a database trace

toolkit.what: Translate a hot query once and reuse it. Saves the LINQ-to-SQL work on every call; worth it only on very frequent queries.
flags: the context and parameters the query takes
compile once for the whole app
toolkit.example:
static readonly Func<AppDb, int, Task<Book?>> ById =
    EF.CompileAsyncQuery((AppDb db, int id) => db.Books.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Id == id));

steps.prompt: A security review flags this search. A user typed `x' OR 1=1 --`. What is the fix?
options: Use `FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Books WHERE Title = {title}")` so the value is sent as a parameter
Switch to `FromSqlInterpolated` but keep the quotes around `{title}`
steps.explain: `FromSqlRaw` takes the string as it is, so the interpolation pastes user text into SQL. `FromSql` turns each `{value}` into a parameter. Do not put quotes around the placeholder: the parameter is already a value, not text in the SQL.

steps.prompt: Match each API to its job.
pairs: no tracking, one object per row
a comment in the SQL to find it later

steps.prompt: A read-only list for an API: tag it, do not track it, and read only three columns.
What does the first line of the generated SQL say?
code: class Order { public int Id { get; set; } public int Total { get; set; } }
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder o) => o.UseSqlite("Data Source=:memory:");
steps.explain: `TagWith` adds the text as a SQL comment before the SELECT. In a slow-query report, that line tells you which page sent the query.

Load a user and add a role to them
steps.explain: Tracking is what lets `SaveChanges` find your edits. If you are not going to save, do not pay for it.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Write read paths as `AsNoTracking` or `Select` projections and tag every query that matters with `TagWith`. Never build SQL text from user input: if you need raw SQL, use `FromSql` with interpolated values, and read the SQL with `ToQueryString()` before review.
